title: How a Healthcare Provider Built HL7v2® and FHIR® Interoperability on Snowflake
summary: See how SDG Group built real-time HL7v2 and FHIR data ingestion on Snowflake using Snowpark Container Services and Snowflake Postgres.
body_markdown:
Healthcare moves at the speed of care. A patient is transferred between facilities, a surgeon updates a protocol, a therapist logs an observation — these events happen in real time. Yet for decades, the systems meant to make sense of that activity have lagged behind it, learning about a transfer, a referral or a missed appointment only after a batch file lands. It could be hours, days or sometimes weeks before that information arrives.


That gap between the moment care happens and the moment an organization can act on it is one of the most persistent problems in healthcare. Closing that gap does more than optimize operations — it's what allows an organization to shift from reacting to patient needs to anticipating them in the moment.


That shift is exactly what one of our customers, a healthcare provider, set out to achieve. It's a case study in what's possible when you build interoperability on top of a unified data and AI platform rather than bolting it on after the fact.


## Legacy challenges: fragmentation, delays and added cost


Like many multisite healthcare organizations, this provider worked across a patchwork of electronic health record (EHR) and electronic medical record (EMR) systems from its many hospital partners. To make sense of it all, the organization relied on third-party data-as-a-service vendors to consolidate that data and deliver prebuilt KPIs and dashboards into a Snowflake instance it already owned.


The arrangement had real limits. The organization didn't control the business logic behind its own KPIs. Data refreshes could lag a week to a month due to gaps in the source feeds, which meant decisions about clinical efficiency, patient outcomes, resource allocation and revenue were being made in hindsight rather than in the moment. And the bill for that lack of control kept climbing.


The turning point came when the organization decided to enable proactive action through seamless access to data from its hospital partners.


## Building the solution: supporting HL7® FHIR® interoperability on Snowflake


Rather than adding a separate, standalone HL7v2® integration engine, Snowflake and SDG Group proposed something different: build the interoperability layer directly on the unified data and AI platform the organization already owned and trusted.


The architecture combines several Snowflake capabilities working together. Snowpark Container Services runs the ingestion layer that receives HL7v2® messages — admissions, discharge, transfers and scheduled visits feeds — from hospital partners' EHRs. Because that transactional, message-based traffic needed an OLTP-style landing zone, the team used Snowflake Postgres as the intake layer before pushing data down into Snowflake itself. An interface engine layer gives the provider's own analysts direct control over field mapping, so the organization decides how incoming HL7v2® and Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®) data gets structured and trusted.


Security was foundational, not an afterthought. The provider was still maturing its own security and compliance program, so the team designed the solution to take advantage of Snowflake's security and governance capabilities, including encryption of data at rest within its Azure environment. The team is now extending Snowflake Horizon's auto-classification and dynamic masking to keep access tightly governed as more data and more hospital partners come online. Additionally, they plan to leverage Snowflake’s managed data mirroring capability for seamless data movement between Snowflake Postgres (OLTP) and native Snowflake (OLAP).


"Our client didn't need another integration engine standing between them and their data — they needed to own it outright, as their own intellectual property," said Luveen Arolkar, Senior Director, Data Management and Alliances Lead at SDG Group. "By building the interoperability layer natively on Snowflake, we gave their team full control over how every HL7v2® message is mapped and validated — turning data they once waited weeks for into data they can act on the same day. And we engineered it to scale: each new hospital partner builds on the same foundation."


## The results: faster invoice recognition, closed gaps in care and a foundation built for scale


The impact has been both operational and financial. The organization now captures HL7v2® messages in near real time, eliminating the truncation issues it saw with its previous feeds. Its own analysts trust the data enough to act on it because they control how it's mapped and validated. That trust has translated into concrete gains: The organization reports more efficient invoice recognition, while it's layering in provider incentive automation that wasn't possible when data lagged by weeks. The foundation also opens the door to referral-to-evaluation tracking, readmission-pattern analysis and bidirectional data exchange, where care plan updates and therapy observations flow back to referring hospitals and surgeons in near real time, closing the loop on patient progress.


Just as important, the architecture is designed to be extensible: New hospital partners can connect to the same foundation, typically with interface mapping rather than a new pipeline, depending on the EHR configuration.


## Why this matters beyond one organization


This project is just a preview of where healthcare interoperability has the potential to go. HL7v2® and other interoperability formats like FHIR® and Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture (C-CDA) have traditionally been treated as operational: a message pushed from one healthcare entity to the next with little examination of what it actually contains. But when that data lands on a platform like Snowflake, it becomes something more: a near real-time input into a broader, evolving picture of patient health, one that can be enriched with social determinants of health, AI-driven classification and other context the platform already holds. It's less a pass-through integration and more the foundation of a living data mesh — and the same pattern extends beyond HL7v2® to FHIR®, C-CDA, X12 and whatever interoperability standards come next.


“The gap between a health event and the action it should trigger has hindered healthcare outcomes for a generation. Closing that gap requires a system of intelligence to turn into a system of action — and it's the difference between an organization that reacts to care and one that keeps pace with it.” —Jeevan Rag, Global Healthcare CTO, Snowflake
